application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: It is unrealistic to assume that a computer system will never fail. Yet, there is no fault-free system. Nevertheless, even in the presence of possible faults, the system should continue operating as normal as possible and it is not expected to crash. That assertion is especially true for hard real-time systems on which human lives may depend on. Considering this scenario, this paper introduces a computational and conceptual model addressing the fault resilience improvement in a class of hard real-time system named avionics systems. Essentially, the proposed computational and conceptual model consists of a fundamental schedulability analysis and three other different algorithms. This paper shows the improvement of fault resilience, on up to 80%, by composing and applying space and time redundancy (i.e., multiprocessors and scheduling) with task migration among processors in hard real-time systems' design.

div.head: Main Related Works
div.p: According to [2], despite the fact multi-core processors are around since years ago, developing algorithms that effectively takes advantage of hardware parallelism is still quite challenging.
[3] proposed a reconfiguration mechanism based on multi-version tasks, which leads the system to a maximum benefit at runtime.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Fault tolerance can be understood as a generic term that describes redundant design techniques with duplicated components or repeated computations, so that the system can continue operating (i.e., tolerant) in response to a component failure (i.e., fault) [1]. Redundancy is assumed as basis for fault tolerance.

Considering this context, this paper addresses the fault resilience improvement of a specific computer system class named hard real-time system. A fail in this kind of system may be unacceptable, since it almost always involves human lives. Therefore, hard real-time systems have to supply the correct output at the correct time frame.

The main paper goal is to investigate means to improve fault resilience in hard real-time systems. With regard to this objective, the following hypothesis was formulated: Fault resilience can be improved by composing and applying space and time redundancy (i.e., multiprocessors and scheduling) with task migration among processors in hard real-time systems' design.

The proposed solution resides in the field of off-line guarantee. The tests (schedulability or feasibility analysis) are conducted at the system design time considering a priority-based fashion. This alternative aims a deterministic predictability, since the computational load has to be known a priori (i.e., design time). In this case, no task is rejected in the system. If a fault takes place, for instance, a substitute task with less functionality is dispatched aiming to prevent the system from crashing. In spite of having none of the task's functions executed, the system has at least a minimum core executed by a substitute task.

Hard-real time systems (as a major area), more specifically the avionics are considered the target of this research work. Coping with this system class requires fault tolerance adoption, due to the involved complexity. In this work, it is aimed to be achieved by applying space and time redundancy together.

The remainder of this paper brings the main works related to this one, a basic background, the main paper contribution which is the computational and conceptual model (C2M), an illustrative example, the obtained results, and the paper conclusion.

div.head: Background
div.p: This section intends to introduce the main concepts used along with this research work. Briefly, it includes real-time systems, tasks, fault tolerance, multiprocessors and uniprocessor, scheduling, and scheduling tests.

div.head: Real-Time Systems
div.p: These systems have to output the right value at the right time. It means that system correctness depends also on the time a result is produced, besides the logical computation [14].

Soft real-time systems have more flexible time constraints and do not offer any risk to human lives. Conversely, hard real-time systems have to strictly obey their time constraints. Should it fail to give right results on time, high costs are involved, including human lives.

Basically, real-time timeliness requirements are specified in terms of task deadlines, which are the maximum time tasks should be completely executed. Depending on the consequences a missed deadline may cause, it is called hard, soft, or firm. Time is the main aspect that differs real-time systems from others. Also, this term is strictly related to the environment a system operates. The term real indicates that a system reaction to the external events should happen during their evolution. Moreover, real-time does not implies fast-time response [14].

div.head: Tasks
div.p: A task can be considered as a computation executed by a processor in a sequential order. Some authors consider tasks to be the most important software entity treated by an operating system [6].

div.head: 6A2-3
div.p: When task's activations occur in an infinite sequence, but following a regular interval between one activation and other, this task is said periodic. Each activation is considered as a task instance. In this case, all task release times are known.

On the other hand, when there is no a priori knowledge about task arrival times, and there is no regular time for task activation, this task is said aperiodic. This type of task comes to execute in a random fashion. The sporadic tasks represent a variation of the aperiodic ones.

div.head: Fault Tolerance
div.p: According to [1], fault tolerance computing means computing correctly despite the existence of errors in a system. The role of fault tolerance mechanism is to cover the safety aspects. It means to avoid failures in the presence of faults [15].
A system is said fault-tolerant if it produces correct results even when faults occur [16]. Fault tolerance is closely related to redundancy mechanisms.

The N-version is the most common fault tolerant software used in avionics systems. On the other hand, analytical redundancy (reconfigurable controls) are one emerging concept [17]. Nevertheless, it is not possible to tolerate every single fault a system may has. Then, a failure hypothesis stipulates how faults affect the behavior of a given system.

div.head: Multiprocessor vs. Uniprocessor
div.p: There are much more results available in the literature about uniprocessor than multiprocessor, since complexity results show that most real-time multiprocessing scheduling is NP-hard [18].

According to [19], a fundamental restriction in multiprocessor real-time scheduling is that a single job may execute upon at most one processor at any instant in time, even if there are several idle processors available.
Moreover, [20] points out that the understanding of real-time multiprocessor scheduling has lagged behind that of uniprocessor scheduling.

There are many ways on which a multiprocessor system can be built. Nevertheless, the symmetric multiprocessor (SMP) arrangement is the most common one. It considers several identical processors sharing access to memories, Input/Outputs (I/O) devices, and other needed peripherals.
By comparing multiprocessor scheduling with uniprocessor, a first significant result found is a theorem stating the absence of optimality of on-line scheduling algorithms [21]:

div.head: Theorem 1
div.p: An on-line algorithm which builds a feasible schedule for any set of tasks with deadlines within m processors (m ≥ 2), cannot exist.
Next, there is a theorem related to the schedule length, which is the same for uniprocessor-based systems [22].

div.head: Theorem 2
div.p: There is a feasible schedule for a set of periodic and independent tasks if and only if there is a feasible schedule in the time interval given by [𝑟 𝑚𝑖𝑛 , 𝑟 𝑚𝑎𝑥 + 𝜀 ], where 𝑟 𝑚𝑖𝑛 = 𝑀𝑖𝑛{𝑟 𝑖 } , 𝑟 𝑚𝑎𝑥 = 𝑀𝑎𝑥{𝑟 𝑖 } , 𝜀 = 𝐿𝐶𝑀{𝑇 𝑖 }, and i ∈ [1, n]. [23] states that: "For a multiprocessor system, if a schedule exists that meets the deadlines of a set of single-instance tasks whose start times are the same, then the same set of tasks can be scheduled at run-time even if their start times are different and not known a priori".
Moreover, considering the case with 𝑛 periodic and independent tasks to execute in 𝑚 processors, another conclusion is the necessary condition:
div.formula: 𝑈 = ∑ 𝑚 𝑗=1 𝑈 𝑗 = ∑ 𝑛 𝑖=1 𝑢 𝑖 = ∑ 𝑛 𝑖=1 𝐶 𝑖 𝑃 𝑖
div.p: ≤ 𝑚, where 𝑢 𝑖 is the utilization factor of task 𝑖; 𝐶 𝑖 is the computation time; and 𝑃 𝑖 is the period of a single task.
[22] states the necessary schedulability condition referring to the maximum processor utilization factor (𝑈 𝑗 ) of each processor

div.head: Scheduling
div.p: A scheduling algorithm should be capable to determine when to execute which task at which order. When a multiprocessor or distributed system is used, it has also to determine tasks assignment to specific processors [23]. According to this author, scheduling is the central activity of a computer system, generally performed by a given operating system. The main goal is to keep up with all task's deadlines.

div.head: 6A2-4
div.p: Considering that context, schedulability analysis aims to verify whether a given set of tasks together with its specified constraints can be successfully scheduled by a given scheduling algorithm.

A scheduling algorithm is named off-line if it generates a schedule based on the entire task set before task activation. The on-line algorithm creates a new schedule every time a new task enters the system or a running task terminates. Off-line algorithms should be applied in design time always, since they represent a schedulability analysis part.

div.head: Scheduling Tests
div.p: Scheduling tests are executed to verify whether a task set is schedulable. Tests varies according to task model and scheduling policy. Generally, testing is the worst case analysis. In some cases tests are found to be NP.

According to [24], scheduling tests may be separated into sufficient, exact, and necessary tests. Sufficient test is considered simple test, however, it can discard tasks from the feasible task set. Accepted tasks are always schedulable. Exact test is a precise test in identifying non-schedulable tasks. This analysis does not reject schedulable tasks. In many cases this test is not practicable. Necessary test is simple analysis and not so restrictive. A task set evaluated by this analysis does not necessarily means a feasible scheduling. This only guarantee that all rejected task is not feasible to schedule.

For instance, [23] states that given a set of 𝑘 independent, preemptable (at discrete time instants), and periodic tasks on a multiprocessor system with 𝑛 processors considering 𝑈 = ∑ 𝑘 𝑖=1 𝐶 𝑖 𝑃 𝑖 ≤ 𝑛 , let
div.formula: 𝑇 = 𝐺𝐶𝐷(𝑃 1 , ⋯ , 𝑃 𝑘 ) and 𝑡 = 𝐺𝐶𝐷(𝑇, 𝑇 × ( 𝐶 1 𝑃 1 ), ⋯ , 𝑇 × ( 𝐶 𝑘 𝑃 𝑘 )).
div.p: When 𝑡 is integral, this represents a sufficient condition for a feasible scheduling considering this task set.

div.head: The Proposed Computational and Conceptual Model (C2M)
div.p: C2M is composed by two main parts. The first one is the computational part which formally defines how the system has to be modelled. It is the static part.
The second one is the conceptual part, which defines how the system behaves. It is the dynamic part.

The computational part presents the developed system task model, the adopted fault model, and scheduling considerations. The conceptual part tackles the proposed schedulability analysis and three algorithms named Fixed-Priority based Scheduling Algorithm (FPSA), Symmetric Multiprocessor-based Dispatcher Algorithm (SMP-DA), and Fault Tolerance Algorithm (FTA).

div.head: Assumptions
div.p: The system task model is as close to real world as possible. Considering this premise, periodic, aperiodic, and sporadic tasks are taken into account.
To achieve the previous stated proposition, the following assumptions have to be considered:
• There are periodic, sporadic, and aperiodic tasks in the system; • All tasks are fully preemptable;

• The system is symmetric multiprocessor-based; • Tasks are scheduled as per fixed-priority fashion (different priority assignments may affect the system timeliness aspect); and • There are no precedence constraints among tasks.

div.head: C2M Analysis
div.p: Next, it follows two analysis. The first considers aspects on symmetric and asymmetric multiprocessor-based. The seconds tackles task precedence issues.

div.head: Symmetric vs. Asymmetric
div.p: Taking into account assumption (A3), there is an important point behind the stage that needs some attention. An asymmetric multiprocessor-based system requires as many versions of tasks 𝜏 as the number of different processors 𝜓 the system possesses. Suppose a system has 𝑚 processors types and 𝑛 tasks. The task set would be Γ = (𝜏 1,1 , … , 𝜏 𝑖,𝑗 ), where 0 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑛 and 0 ≤ 𝑗 ≤ 𝑚 . Moreover, the scheduler and the dispatcher algorithms would have to perform some considerable extra computing. They have to assign a given task 𝜏 𝑖𝑗 to an available processor type 𝜓 𝑗 (i.e., which matches the task type).

div.head: 6A2-5
div.p: Each individual task 𝜏 𝑖𝑗 needs its Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) to be calculated.

Besides the time overhead, the space would also be a constraint. Considering the target system for this work is an avionic system, the developers would have to build 𝑚 versions of the system and embed all of them into the mission computer. The cost to develop, test, verify, and validate that system would be significantly impacted causing it to be quite not feasible.

Therefore, symmetric multiprocessor-based opens up the possibility that system performance can be improved if tasks execute immediately on available resources instead of waiting for resources best suited to the task type.

div.head: Task Precedence
div.p: Another point is about assumption (A5), where the following lemma can be originated.

div.head: Lemma 3
div.p: There is no real relevance in having or not dependence (i.e., precedence constraints) among tasks for C2M.

div.head: Proof
div.p: Let's suppose it has. In this case, task A needs task B to run before it in order to produce some data task A is waiting for consume. Both tasks, A (consumer) and B (producer), may have the same priority. What will be important in this case is the period they run. If the system designer does not attribute the correct period of execution to those tasks, what would happen is: (i) task A does not have anything for consume and then it leaves the processor for other task to execute; (ii) task B does not have any free slot on its buffer to put the data it produces and then it leaves the processor for other task to execute and some data are lost as long as this situation remains. Now, let's suppose there is no dependence between tasks A and B. Thus, they will execute independently from each other and they will leave the processor as soon as they do not require it (i.e., tasks are complete) or are not able to continue for any reason. Therefore, for both cases the major problem, in this conceptual work scenario, would be a temporal fault, rather than precedence constraint. Temporal faults shall be off-line worked out by means of schedulability analysis. Finally, the scheduler will always select the first task from the ready queue to execute next.
Considering Lemma 3 and without losing generality, the tasks used afterwards will have no precedence constraints, just for the sake of simplicity.

div.head: Periodic Task Model
div.p: The periodic task model considers a set Π = {𝜋 1 , 𝜋 2 , ⋯ , 𝜋 𝑛 } of n periodic tasks. The point of this task model is to split each task 𝜋 𝑖 (0 < 𝑖 ≤ 𝑛) into a periodic task job set. Therefore, 𝜋 𝑖 comprises a set 𝐾 𝑖 = { 𝜅 𝑖1 , 𝜅 𝑖2 , ⋯ , 𝜅 𝑖𝑥 } of 𝑥 𝑖 periodic jobs. This technique also applies to sporadic and aperiodic task model. It gives the possibility of having a configurable granularity control.

A periodic job 𝜅 𝑖𝑞 = {𝐶 𝑖𝑞 , 𝑇 𝑖 , 𝐷 𝑖𝑞 , 𝜂 𝑖𝑞 , 𝛾 𝑖 } (0 < 𝑞 ≤ 𝑥 𝑖 ), where 𝐶 𝑖𝑞 stands for the WCET, 𝑇 𝑖 for the period, 𝐷 𝑖𝑞 for the relative deadline, 𝜂 𝑖𝑞 for the relative notification time (NT), and 𝛾 𝑖 for the task priority.

The total execution time 𝐶 𝑖 of 𝜋 𝑖 is ∑ 𝑥 𝑖 𝑞=1 𝐶 𝑖𝑞 . For a periodic task, it does not matter how many jobs it has when the subject is the task period. Even though the task is split, the period of execution is the same for each one of the 𝑥 𝑖 periodic jobs. It is inherited from 𝜋 𝑖 . Then 𝑇 𝑖 = 𝑇 𝑖1 , ⋯ , 𝑇 𝑖𝑞 , where 0 < 𝑞 ≤ 𝑥 𝑖 .

Deadlines for periodic jobs are considered hard real-time, which means no periodic job is supposed to miss its deadline. The total relative deadline 𝐷 𝑖 of 𝜋 𝑖 is ∑ 𝑥 𝑖 𝑞=1 𝐷 𝑖𝑞 . Each periodic job 𝜅 𝑖𝑞 has its own individual relative NT 𝜂 𝑖𝑞 .
Analogous to the task period, the task priority is the same for all 𝑞 periodic jobs, 𝛾 𝑖 = 𝛾 𝑖1 , ⋯ , 𝛾 𝑖𝑞 .
The periodic task set Π is supposed to execute within a major cycle 𝑃, where 𝑃 = 𝐿𝐶𝑀(𝑇 𝑖 , ⋯ , 𝑇 𝑛 ).
Tasks shall respect the rule 0 < 𝐶 𝑖𝑞 ≤ 𝐷 𝑖𝑞 ≤ 𝑇 𝑖 .

div.head: Aperiodic Task Model
div.p: The aperiodic task model considers a set 𝐴 = {𝛼 1 , 𝛼 2 , ⋯ , 𝛼 𝑚 } of m aperiodic tasks. An aperiodic task 𝛼 𝑗 (0 < 𝑗 ≤ 𝑚) comprises a set of 𝐽 𝑗 = {𝜌 𝑗1 , 𝜌 𝑗2 , ⋯ , 𝜌 𝑗𝑘 } of 𝑘 𝑗 jobs.

div.head: 6A2-6
div.p: An aperiodic job 𝜌 𝑗𝑤 = {𝐶 ̆𝑗𝑤 , 𝐷 � 𝑗𝑤 , 𝜂 � 𝑗𝑤 , 𝛾 � 𝑗 } (0 < 𝑤 ≤ 𝑘 𝑗 ), where 𝐶 ̆𝑗𝑤 stands for the WCET, 𝐷 � 𝑗𝑤 for the relative deadline, 𝜂 � 𝑗𝑤 for relative NT, and 𝛾 � 𝑗 for the priority.

The total execution time 𝐶 ̆𝑗 of 𝛼 𝑗 is ∑ 𝑘 𝑗 𝑤=1 𝐶 ̆𝑗𝑤 . Deadlines for aperiodic jobs are considered soft real-time, which means that missing a deadline is acceptable and causes no major impact in the overall system. The total relative deadline 𝐷 � 𝑗 of 𝛼 𝑗 is
The aperiodic jobs inherit their priority from their originating tasks, as follows:
div.formula: 𝛾 � 𝑗 = 𝛾 � 𝑗1 , ⋯ , 𝛾 � 𝑗𝑤 .
div.p: Tasks shall respect the rule: 0 < 𝐶 ̆𝑗𝑤 ≤ 𝐷 � 𝑗𝑤 .

In this work, it is assumed that aperiodic tasks have soft deadlines. It means that an aperiodic job (i.e., 𝜌 𝑗𝑘 ) is to be executed as soon as possible. Another consideration is actually a fact. The number of aperiodic events occurring during one major cycle 𝑃 is unknown. As aperiodic events are associated with aperiodic jobs, the last is also unknown. In order to cope with this regular and unavoidable case, a probability distribution has to be applied to randomly generate the aperiodic jobs number occurring within 𝑃.

By observing the dynamic of a given system, it is possible to derive the behavior of aperiodic events for the schedulability analysis. The jobs comprising an aperiodic task are alike regarding statistical behavior and timing requirements. Then, their inter-arrival times can be distributed random variables.
As long as the system statistical behavior and its environment do not change, the system is said stationary. This concept holds in time periods of length on the order of 𝑃.

Therefore, the number 𝑚 of aperiodic tasks is unknown during the major period 𝑃. Although, 𝑚′ can be obtained by a probability distribution which represents the actual behavior of the system: 𝑚′ = 𝑃𝑜𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑛𝐷𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑏𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛(𝐴𝑝𝑒𝑟𝑖𝑜𝑑𝑖𝑐𝑇𝑎𝑠𝑘𝑠).

The Poisson distribution [25] is applied here to expresses the probability of a given number of aperiodic tasks occurring in a fixed time interval, which is 𝑃. It is assumed that the average rate the events occur is known and they occur independently from the time since last event happened. This distribution was selected because it was considered the most suitable to represent the nature of the problem: "express the probability of an event take place within a time frame".

div.head: Sporadic Task Model
div.p: The sporadic task model considers a set Δ = {𝛿 1 , 𝛿 2 , ⋯ , 𝛿 𝑧 } of z sporadic tasks. An sporadic task 𝛿 𝑙 (0 < 𝑙 ≤ 𝑧) comprises a set of Θ 𝑙 = {𝜃 𝑙1 , 𝜃 𝑙2 , ⋯ , 𝜃 𝑙𝑦 } of 𝑦 𝑙 jobs.
A sporadic job 𝜃 𝑙𝑟 = {𝐶 𝑙𝑟 , 𝐷 𝑙𝑟 , 𝜂 𝑙𝑟 , 𝛾 𝑙 } (0 < 𝑟 ≤ 𝑦 𝑙 ) , where 𝐶 𝑙𝑟 stands for the WCET, 𝐷 𝑙𝑟 for the relative deadline, 𝜂 𝑙𝑟 for relative NT, and 𝛾 𝑙 for the priority.

The total execution time 𝐶 𝑙 of 𝛿 𝑙 is ∑ 𝑦 𝑙 𝑟=1 𝐶 𝑙𝑟 . Deadlines for sporadic jobs are considered hard real-time, which means no sporadic job is supposed to miss its deadline.The total relative deadline 𝐷 𝑙 of 𝛿 𝑙 is ∑ 𝑦 𝑙 𝑟=1 𝐷 𝑙𝑟 .
The sporadic jobs inherit their priority from their originating tasks, as follows:
div.formula: 𝛾 𝑙 = 𝛾 𝑙1 , ⋯ , 𝛾 𝑙𝑟 .
div.p: Tasks shall respect the rule: 0 < 𝐶 𝑙𝑟 ≤ 𝐷 𝑙𝑟 .

While aperiodic tasks have soft deadlines, sporadic tasks have hard deadlines. Furthermore, the number of sporadic events occurring in a major cycle given by 𝑃 is unknown. As sporadic events are associated with sporadic jobs, the last is also unknown (the number 𝑧 of sporadic jobs).
By similarity to the aperiodic events, 𝑧′ can be obtained by applying a probability distribution representing the actual behavior of the system: 𝑧′ = 𝑃𝑜𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑜𝑛𝐷𝑖𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑏𝑢𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛(𝑆𝑝𝑜𝑟𝑎𝑑𝑖𝑐𝑇𝑎𝑠𝑘𝑠).

div.head: Resources
div.p: The C2M considers a set Ψ = {𝜓 1 , 𝜓 2 , ⋯ , 𝜓 𝑝 } of 𝑝 processors as resources.

div.head: Fault Model (FM)
div.p: This work considers only the transient and intermittent types of faults for the FM.

Generally, some researches assume a fixed number of faults that may occur in a given system. This could lead to a pessimistic design directly impacting tasks response times. One alternative to this 6A2-7 is using a stochastic process with a Poisson distribution. It has been traditionally accepted as a reasonable assumption for the arrival of transient faults [4]. Therefore, the Poisson model has been adopted as the FM for C2M.

div.head: Schedulability Analysis
div.p: The conceptual model mechanism is about arranging tasks so that they could be assigned to execute on up to one processor at a time. Eventual faults may take place and affect tasks which are in execution. When this case occurs, the faulty task has to be stopped in order to give room to a substitute task with less functionality compared to the former.

At first, all task kinds have to pass the schedulability analysis. The main purpose of this analysis is to evaluate whether tasks are able to complete before their deadlines according to the scheduling algorithm.

One of the mechanisms implemented here to verify if a fault occurred is the NT control. It involves all kinds of tasks (𝜂 for 𝜋, 𝜂 � for 𝜌, and 𝜂 for 𝜃). The NT is a control point (i.e., milestone) a task has to inform in order to communicate it has no problem on its execution path. If it does not inform its specified NT, a recovery procedure takes place. The NT is detailed in the FTA section.

The solution proposed in this research work resides in the field of off-line guarantee. Tests, which are the schedulability analysis, has to be conducted at the system design time considering a priority-based fashion. This alternative aims a deterministic predictability, since the computational load has to be known a priori (i.e., design time). In this case, no task shall be rejected in the system.
In order to carry on the schedulability analysis, it is assumed all tasks are released at time 0. The behavior is then repeated every major cycle 𝑃.
Notice that tasks properties are used to derive the conditions stated in this analysis.

In the proposed conceptual model, task servers [22] are employed to schedule both aperiodic and sporadic tasks. Polling server technique attend to aperiodic tasks and Sporadic server to sporadic tasks. Provided that servers have capacity, they can take advantage of the same schedulability tests applied for periodic tasks. This is possible by assuming their capacity times as execution times, without losing generality.

Therefore, the number of aperiodic and sporadic tasks shall be obtained through Poisson distribution. Polling server comprises a period 𝑇 𝑃𝑆 and a capacity 𝐶 𝑃𝑆 and Sporadic server comprises a period 𝑇 𝑆𝑆 and a capacity 𝐶 𝑆𝑆 .

Servers period must be the shortest periodic task period ( 𝑇 𝑆𝑆 = 𝑇 𝑃𝑆 = 𝑀𝑖𝑛{𝑇 𝑖 } ). This guarantee the server to run at the maximum target system rate in order to not miss aperiodic and sporadic events. Moreover, it does not jeopardize the periodic tasks performance nor execution because by the nature of servers, if there is no event to serve, they will not be schedule to execute.
On the other hand, server capacity have to be the longest execution time from aperiodic, 𝐶 𝑃𝑆 = 𝑀𝑎𝑥{𝐶 ̆𝑗𝑤 } and 𝐶 𝑆𝑆 = 𝑀𝑎𝑥{𝐶 𝑙𝑟 }.
Moving on, three schedulability tests have to be applied in the periodic task set: (i) necessary test, (ii) first sufficient test, and (iii) second sufficient test.

The test (i) guarantees that all the rejected task are not feasible to schedule. Therefore, if the task set does not pass in this test, it should be redesigned until the condition holds. That is considered the goal of this step, i.e., task set tuning.

div.head: Definition (i)
div.p: Necessary Condition. In order to verify whether the periodic, aperiodic, and sporadic task sets are able to execute considering a minimum number of 𝑝 processors, the following necessary condition must hold: 𝑈 +

div.p: The Necessary Condition (i) is immediate. If the total utilization factor is > 𝑝, there is no feasible schedule for that task set.

div.p: The condition (i) was extended to consider also aperiodic and sporadic tasks. This extension does not compromise the validity of the former equation, since aperiodic and sporadic tasks are being handled throughout the server technique. Servers have the same attributes of periodic tasks.

div.p: Whenever the execution time is equal to the relative deadline for all periodic tasks and server capacity is equal to the relative deadline for aperiodic and sporadic tasks, a sufficient condition is made, provided condition (i) holds. div.head: FPSA
div.p: This algorithm considers all active tasks (periodic, aperiodic, and sporadic) in order to produce a feasible schedule and arrange it in a ready queue. The FPSA is on-line performed and partitioned model based.

As implicit, considering hard real-time systems, no task can be rejected and a feasible schedule has to be generated. Therefore, at this point the schedulability analysis has to be already performed, so that any temporal fault the given system may have is solved.
The algorithm starts with the system counting time process which is monitored via 𝑇𝑖𝑐𝑘 𝐹𝑃𝑆𝐴 . When the target system is powered-up, 𝑇𝑖𝑐𝑘 𝐹𝑃𝑆𝐴 is linked 6A2-9
to the system tick control and it is updated whenever the last is updated.

As periodic tasks are hard real-time, FPSA goes through the periodic tasks set Π first and looks for all tasks that are ready to execute considering its period. Then, those tasks are entered into the 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦𝑄𝑢𝑒𝑢𝑒 𝐹𝑃𝑆𝐴 according to its priority. Moreover, as soon as a sporadic 𝜃 𝑙 or a aperiodic 𝛼 𝑗 tasks arise they are served by the Sporadic or Polling servers.

Next, both Sporadic and Aperiodic servers are entered into the 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦𝑄𝑢𝑒𝑢𝑒 𝐹𝑃𝑆𝐴 according to its periods. Should no sporadic or aperiodic tasks be ready to be served, server just gives up the processor utilization when they are dispatched to execute.
A given task enters into the 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦𝑄𝑢𝑒𝑢𝑒 𝐹𝑃𝑆𝐴 in a position according to its priority.
The FPSA result is the 𝑅𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑦𝑄𝑢𝑒𝑢𝑒 𝐹𝑃𝑆𝐴 , which is the base for the SMP-DA.

div.head: SMP-DA
div.p: This algorithm considers the current ready queue as input. Then, it has to take into account processor utilization factor to assign the ready tasks to a given processor 𝜓.

According to the proposed scheduling strategy, each individual task ( 𝜋 𝑖 , 𝛼 𝑗 , or 𝛿 𝑙 ) has to be scheduled to execute in just one processor 𝜓 𝑝 at a time. Thus, it is not allowed to execute two different jobs from the same task in parallel.

Dispatching is the action of choosing which task to execute next on a processor. As this work intends to use fixed-priority scheduling policy, the task with the highest priority in the ready queue will be the next task to execute.

The SMP-DA also verifies which processor has more capability to accept that task in that specific time slot. This is based on the processor loading factor 𝑈 of processors. The processor with the lowest 𝑈 is more likely to accept that task.

The SMP-DA considers that eventual task preemptions may occur. However, this algorithm intends to minimize the number of preemptions in the system by applying the waiting condition. The goal is to check if a ready task can wait for a processor until that processor becomes available and still complete within its deadline.

div.head: Definition
div.p: Waiting Condition. When there is no available processor (𝑈 ≠ 0) in the time 𝑡 to receive a task ready to be dispatched, SMP-DA looks in advance to verify which will be the next processor to become free and calculates the time it will become free. This is possible by going through the processor set Ψ and verifying which is the task the processor is hosting and verifying which is the task remainder execution time, given by 𝑐(𝑡).
In this case, the time a processor will become available 𝑐(𝑡) would be the task start time 𝑠, that is, 𝑐(𝑡) = 𝑠.

Therefore, if the task ready to be dispatched has it dispatch postponed until the time 𝑐(𝑡) and still complete within its deadline, the Waiting Condition is satisfied. This condition is formal defined by: (𝑠 + 𝐶) = 𝑓 ≤ 𝑑 = (𝑟 + 𝐷) , where 𝑓 is the task finishing time; 𝑠 the task start time; 𝐶 the task execution time; 𝑑 the task absolute deadline; 𝑟 the task release time; and 𝐷 the task relative deadline.
Whenever the waiting condition cannot be satisfied, preemption occurs always respecting deadlines.

Another concept used in the SMP-DA is the Job Information Block (JIB). At the moment a task is assigned and then dispatched to execute in a processor, SMP-DA has to enter the job identification index, the assigned processor and the time to check given by 𝑇𝑖𝑐𝑘 𝐹𝑃𝑆𝐴 + 𝜂 . JIB is utilized by FTA to verify the jobs NT.

div.head: FTA
div.p: This algorithm considers the running tasks. Case any fault is identified, a recovery procedure is started.

In this conceptual model, fault identification is possible through the Notification Time (NT) control. This comprehends an original schema included in the formal task definition in order to be a foundation to the fault tolerance mechanism.

Each job of each task (periodic, aperiodic, and sporadic) has its own NT. It consists in a time when the job has to inform it is normally executing. Case nothing is informed by that time (i.e. NT), the conceptual model assumes that job is facing some sort of problem which will prevent it from continuing. Then, that job has to be substituted.

As previously mentioned, 𝜂 𝑖𝑞 , 𝜂 � 𝑗𝑤 , and 𝜂 𝑙𝑟 are all relative NT. The NT absolute value does not take into account the time the job remains stopped after execution, for instance, when it is preempted. Therefore, NT makes sense only when job is executing. Then, the absolute NT is given by last release time of the job (periodic, aperiodic, or sporadic) plus its original relative NT. The following three equations, defines the absolute NT for all tasks types (periodic, aperiodic, and sporadic):
div.formula: 𝑁𝑇 𝐴𝐵𝑆𝑂𝐿𝑈𝑇𝐸 = 𝐿𝑎𝑠𝑡 𝑟 𝑖𝑞 + 𝜂 𝑖𝑞 ;
div.p: 𝑁 � 𝑇 𝐴𝐵𝑆𝑂𝐿𝑈𝑇𝐸 = 𝐿𝑎𝑠𝑡 𝑟 𝑗𝑤 + 𝜂 � 𝑗𝑤 ; and 𝑁𝑇 𝐴𝐵𝑆𝑂𝐿𝑈𝑇𝐸 = 𝐿𝑎𝑠𝑡 𝑟 𝑙𝑟 + 𝜂 𝑙𝑟 .

The new job is supposed to have less functionality when compared to the former. This implicates in short execution time, since the substituting job has to execute in the time left by the faulty job. That time, which is the execution time of the substituting job, is defined by: 𝐶′ = 𝐶 -𝜂, where 𝐶′ is the execution time of the substitute job; 𝐶 is the WCET of the faulty job; and 𝜂 is the NT of the faulty job.
It is important to notice that 𝜂 defines the maximum execution time a substitute job may have to try a recovery in the target system which is currently operating in a degraded condition.
According to 𝐶′ + 𝜂 ≤ 𝐷, the faulty job relative deadline 𝐷 is still respected.
The substitute job is a one-shot job inheriting the same priority of the job it is related to. Therefore, each task job has just one substitute job which executes just once.
A periodic job 𝜅 𝑖𝑞 has its substitute job defined as: 𝜅′ 𝑖𝑞 = {𝐶′ 𝑖𝑞 , 𝛾 𝑖 } , where 𝐶′ 𝑖𝑞 = 𝐶 𝑖𝑞 -𝜂 𝑖𝑞 and 𝐶′ 𝑖𝑞 ≤ 𝐷 𝑖𝑞 .
An aperiodic job 𝜌 𝑗𝑤 has its substitute job defined as: 𝜌′ 𝑗𝑤 = {𝐶 ̆′𝑗𝑤 , 𝛾 � 𝑗 } , where 𝐶 ̆′𝑗𝑤 = 𝐶 ̆𝑗𝑤 -𝜂 � 𝑗𝑤 and 𝐶 ̆′𝑗𝑤 ≤ 𝐷 � 𝑗𝑤 .

A sporadic job 𝜃 𝑙𝑟 has its substitute job defined as follows: 𝜃′ 𝑙𝑟 = {𝐶′ 𝑙𝑟 , 𝛾 𝑙 }, where 𝐶′ 𝑙𝑟 = 𝐶 𝑙𝑟 -𝜂 𝑙𝑟 and 𝐶′ 𝑙𝑟 ≤ 𝐷 𝑙𝑟 . Therefore, once a fault is detected, aided by NT control, the faulty job is stopped and removed from execution and then two recovery alternatives are verified. The first attempt is to migrate that fault task part, through a substitute job, to another processor, considering the migration condition is satisfied. This opens up the possibility to also execute a recovery procedure specifically for the processor which had the tasks migrated from. For instance, if the fault is related to memory issues, the processor will be able to undertake a memory reset or any other action as long as the corrective action lasts the same execution time of the substitute job. However, this subject is beyond this research work scope.

div.head: Definition
div.p: Task Migration Condition. When a fault occurs in the processor 𝜓 𝑎 , where 𝑎 ∈ [1, 𝑝], the migration condition is expressed by:
(1) if there is an idle 𝜓 𝑣 , where 𝑣 ∈ [1, 𝑝] and 𝑣 ≠ 𝑎, then migrate.

(2) otherwise, on the time given by 𝑡, search for the processor 𝜓 𝑣 , where 𝑣 ∈ [1, 𝑝] and 𝑣 ≠ 𝑎, such that 𝑀𝑖𝑛{𝑇 𝜓 𝑣 }. If found, that processor hosting the task with the shortest period is a candidate to receive the migrating task. Then migrate if 𝑡 + 𝐶′ + (𝑐 𝜓 𝑣 (𝑡)) < 𝑑 𝜓 𝑣 , where 𝑡 is the time when FTA checks and realizes that the job did not informed its NT; 𝐶′ is the execution time of substitute job; 𝑐 𝜓 𝑣 (𝑡) is the remainder execution time of the task held by processor considered the candidate to receive the substitute job; and 𝑑 𝜓 = 𝐷 𝜓 𝑣 + 𝑟 𝜓 𝑣 is the absolute deadline.
Should the first attempt fail, the next action is to immediately dispatch the substitute job of the faulty job on the same processor.
It is implicit that the substitute job is supposed to execute in the remainder time slot the faulty job left. All attempts concern task's deadline.

div.head: C2M Schedulability Analysis Result
div.p: At the end of C2M Schedulability Analysis, all three conditions were verified and satisfied. No tasks shall be rejected by the system. This is the prime objective when coping with hard real-time systems, such as avionics systems.

div.head: Algorithms Application
div.p: Once C2M Schedulability Analysis is successfully accomplished, the C2M algorithms can take place. Namely FPSA, SMP-DA, and FTA.
When the schedulability analysis were conduct, three possible scenarios pointed out.

The first scenario, which is proved by design, is the one which states a requirement of 7 processors to execute the defined task sets. Moreover, it considers only the defined 𝑚′ and 𝑧′ for the number of aperiodic and sporadic events occurring all at the same time (𝑡 = 0), then configuring the worst-case.

The second scenario, may consider the result of Necessary Condition (i) to stablish the number of required processor to schedule the defined task sets. Besides, it considers only the defined 𝑚′ and 𝑧′ for the number of aperiodic and sporadic events occurring all at the same time (𝑡 = 0), then configuring the worst-case.

The third scenario, which stresses the system up to its limit capacity, also considers the result of Necessary Condition (i) to stablish the number of required processors. In this case, 5. Furthermore, it considers that both aperiodic and sporadic events will have as many instances as their servers were designed to handle. That is, at each server release, given by its periods, it is assumed an aperiodic and a sporadic event will occur which triggers their related tasks. For all scenarios, periodic jobs are all released at the same time ( 𝑡 = 0 ), which configures the worst-case.

For the fault arrival rate and injection, considering the interval [0, 𝑃 𝑜 ], some assumptions were made. When the subject at glance is avionics system, a representative example of a Line Replaceable Unit (LRU) is the Flight Control Computer (FCC), since it involves a number of safety of flight (SoF) requirements.

Results, Analysis, and Discussion Whenever the target system accommodates more than one processor, FPSA and SMP-DA could run in parallel. Each one in a different processor.
Moving on, for the analysis made in this particular section, FPSA and SMP-DA are being considered as a single entity named C2M Scheduler.

According to theorem 1, it is deduced that no optimal fixed-priority scheduling (on-line) algorithm does exists, since given any fixed-priority algorithm, it is possible to find a schedulable task set that cannot be scheduled by that algorithm. It means that a given algorithm is not capable to cope with, i.e., to produce a feasible schedule given any set of tasks.

Fortunately, there is another theorem that supports a possible closing to that open issue. According to theorem 2, if there is a feasible schedule in a defined time interval, there is a feasible schedule for that task set, as also mentioned by [22].
The same manner C2M Schedulability Analysis is off-line performed, C2M Scheduler is also off-line performed, as follows.

As stated by theorem 1, there is not a magical algorithm able to deal with all kind of tasks. On the other hand, supported by the C2M Schedulability Analysis and by theorem 2, C2M Scheduler can be proved.

The C2M Schedulability Analysis defines the task sets to be submitted to C2M Scheduler. At the end, even the aperiodic and sporadic tasks are treated as periodic tasks once the server technique are employed. Thus, task sets are within the range covered by the theorems 1 and 2.
C2M Scheduler is off-line performed just once considering the worst-case scenario configured when all tasks are dispatched at the same time with 𝑡 = 0:

The time interval considered to C2M Scheduler is given by [0, 𝑃 𝑜 ]. Therefore, if C2M Scheduler is able to off-line produce a feasible schedule for that conditions, C2M Scheduler can produce a feasible schedule also on-line and considering different release times.
Following the same principle of FPSA and SMP-DA, whenever the target system accommodates more than two processors, those algorithms could run in parallel. Each one in a different processor.

Very briefly, FTA checks its input which is the 𝐽𝐼𝐵 𝑆𝑀𝑃𝐷𝐴 to verify the NT of jobs. Whenever there is a NT on that time 𝑡 , FTA verifies if the job has informed its NT. Otherwise, it indicates that a recovery procedures has to be immediately taken considering FTA criteria.
The schedule length for all experiments were given by [0, 𝑃 𝑜 ], and 𝑃 𝑜 = 400 time units.

div.head: Experiment I
div.p: It has considered 7 processors to execute the defined task sets and just one instance of aperiodic 6A2-14 ( 𝑚′ = 1 ) and sporadic ( 𝑧′ = 1 ) events. Those definitions came from the C2M Schedulability Analysis overall result.

div.head: Experiment II
div.p: It has considered 5 processors to execute the defined task sets and just one instance of aperiodic ( 𝑚′ = 1 ) and sporadic ( 𝑧′ = 1 ) events. The total number of processor came from a partial result of C2M Schedulability Analysis, stated by Necessary Condition (i). It aims to verify if it is possible to decrease the required number of processor in the system.

div.head: Experiment III
div.p: This one aimed to stress the system up to its capacity limit, and it also considered the result of Necessary Condition (i) (partial result of C2M Schedulability) to stablish the number of required processors. In this case, 5. Furthermore, it assumed that both aperiodic and sporadic events will have as many instances as their servers were designed to handle. That is, at each server release, given by its periods, it is assumed an aperiodic and a sporadic event will occur which triggers their related task jobs.

div.head: Experiments Phases
div.p: Each experiment was subject to two different phases, as follows.

div.head: First Phase
div.p: Without the presence of faults, the three experiments were submitted to FPSA and SMP-DA. No tasks preemptions nor migration was needed for those task sets scheduling.

For experiment I, II, and III, FPSA and SMP-DA had produced a feasible schedule. This fact (i.e., when FPSA and SMP-DA had produced a feasible schedule for the task sets by using just a partial result of C2M Schedulability Analysis) shows that the Necessary Condition (i) becomes also a sufficient condition, for that specific case. Therefore, for those specific task sets, the total number of processor required in the target system can be decreased from 7 to 5 processors with one instance of an aperiodic event and one instance of an sporadic event occurring within a major cycle 𝑃.

The difference between experiments II and III is that III has considered as many instances of aperiodic and sporadic events as its server were able to cope with, and still be feasible to schedule. Therefore, for those specific task sets, the total number of processor required in the target system can be decreased from 7 to 5 processors with 𝑃 𝑜 𝑇 𝑃𝑆 instances of an aperiodic event and 𝑃 𝑜 𝑇 𝑆𝑆 instances of an sporadic event occurring within a major period 𝑃 𝑜 .

div.head: Second Phase
div.p: Now, considering the presence of faults, the three experiments were submitted to FPSA, SMP-DA, and FTA.

Fault Occurrence Analysis. The number of handled faults, not possible to handle faults, and faults that occurred in an idle processor are shown in Table 6. Regarding experiment I, it has 3 handled faults, 2 faults that were not possible to take a recovery action, and 6 faults hitting an idle processor. Then, by the analysis performed at the last subsection, it can also be concluded that there was a considerable number of time units the processors were in idle state, since there were more that 50% at the total faults dropped in an idle processor.

For experiment II, 4 faults were handled, 1 fault was not possible to be recovered, and 6 others have hit an idle processor. As experiment I, experiment II also had more than 50% of the total number of faults dropping in an empty processor.

In the last experiment, 5 faults were handled, 2 were not possible to handle, and other 4 was caused in a processor which had no tasks being executed at that time fault occurred. Notice that, as experiment III has the greatest processor utilization factor, less faults dropped in an idle processor.
Furthermore, another conclusion is common for all of the three experiments. This is about the notification time 𝜂 definition.

All experiences have shown that when a job has a long execution time (e.g., 𝜅 5,1 and 𝜅 6,1 ) with their notification time defined after a considerable execution time (e.g., 𝜂 5,1 and 𝜂 6,1 ), as illustrated in Table 7, there is a reasonable possibility to have a task with a fault keeping it from executing and a recovery procedure only be started after too long. This way the target system will be in a degraded state until the recovery procedure is undertaken. This situation has occurred only for tasks 𝜋 5 and 𝜋 6 which had a poor task definition.

In order to cope with that issue, C2M suggests task breaking into a meaningful number of jobs, so that jobs will not have too long execution times and by consequence, notification time will be shorter. In this manner, FTA will have its recovery capacity increased and the target system will remain in a jeopardized situation for less time units.

The cases when it was not possible to handle the fault were the ones where the fault occurred after the NT of a job, i.e., even though the job has informed within its specific NT, a fault occurred after that time. Then, linking the concept expressed in the last paragraph, when the task has a meaningful number of jobs per total execution time (e.g., 𝜋 1 ) the side effects are minimized and the system recovery is faster.

div.head: Algorithms Application Result.
div.p: The results presented until this section, has shown both FPSA and SMP-DA were able to generate a feasible schedule considering the overall result of C2M Schedulability Analysis and the considerations mentioned on the beginning of this section. Therefore, their goal is considered achieved.
The Table 8 brings the comparison between the case where FTA was not employed and the case where FTA was employed in the target system, considering those defined task sets.

div.head: 6A2-17
div.p: Regarding Table 8, the header EXP stands for "Experiment", FNH-WOF for "Fault not handled, without FTA", FNH-WF for "Faults not handled, with FTA", HF-WF for "Handled Faults with FTA", and I for "Improvement achieved in %".

By the presented results, it can be noticed that the FTA application has improved the target system fault resilience on up to 80% in the best performance and in at least 60% during its worst performance.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This research work had as main goal the investigation of means to improve fault resilience in hard real-time systems, considering avionics systems as the target.

With regard to this objective, the following hypothesis was formulated: Fault resilience can be improved by composing and applying space and time redundancy (i.e., multiprocessors and scheduling) with task migration among processors in hard real-time systems' design.

This paper introduced a formal model named Computational and Conceptual Model (C2M) to be applied mainly on the hard real-time systems. By using an illustrative example where C2M was fully applied, it was shown that fault resilience was improved on up to 80% by composing and applying space and time redundancy with task migration among processors.

The proposed solution resides in the field of off-line guarantee. The tests (schedulability or feasibility analysis) has to be conducted at the system design time considering a priority-based fashion.
